narrative:
The model predicts you have a 23% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The decision rests mainly on three key aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you do not plan to pursue higher education. Among students who passed, every single one expressed a desire to continue studying after school; your lack of that intention strongly pulls the prediction toward failure. The second most important element is your reason for choosing this school. You selected it for its reputation, a choice shared by only 29% of successful students and one that, in your case, actually works against the prediction of passing. Finally, having no previous class failures is the third factor. This is identical to the average among students who passed and therefore pushes the outcome in a positive direction, though not strongly enough to outweigh the other influences.

Because the top two factors are pulling the model toward failure while only the absence of past failures pulls toward success, the overall prediction tips against you.

To improve, you should seriously reflect on your goals. Reconsidering whether higher education might be right for you could make a real difference. At the same time, look at your very low weekly study time—far below the 2–5 hours that most successful students dedicate—and your high amount of free time and frequent outings with friends. Using some of that time for consistent study could help turn the prediction around.
